Surprisingly, the telescope has discovered a brand new comet, now named C/2026 S1 (Euclid).

They were discovered in 1974, and people have assumed they were built exclusively by men. But new research on this underground army and its chariots, horses and weapons suggests women and children lent a helping hand.

articles.title: Ancient Hox code reveals the developmental roots of vertebrate hind fins and limbs
articles.description: Paired appendages—the pectoral and pelvic fins of fishes and the forelimbs and hindlimbs of tetrapods—were a major innovation in vertebrate evolution. Their emergence greatly expanded the ways vertebrates could move through their environments and ultimately provided the developmental foundation for the evolution of limbs. Yet how the genetic system responsible for building paired appendages was assembled during evolution remains an unresolved question.

articles.description: Scientists have discovered that severely bleached corals can make a remarkable comeback simply by touching healthy, genetically identical corals. articles.title: EU and U.S. Power Firms Scrutinize Supply Chains for Chinese Parts
articles.description: On 1 November, it’s lights-out for power inverters from “high-risk” suppliers to European Union-funded grid projects. The EU will no longer pay for Chinese inverters for these projects, although member nations still can if they so choose. As a result, companies across the EU are reviewing their supply chains and preparing to power their fast-growing grids with fewer Chinese components, which the EU has assessed can enable backdoors to remotely control or shutdown grid infrastructure. The U.S. is enacting its own restrictions for similar reasons. In July, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission added power inverters to its list of foreign technologies that require certification before sale in the country. Then, in August, the White House issued a more expansive executive order banning foreign inverters, transformers, battery storage, generators, and software and firmware. The order also asserts federal authority to review and modify existing installed equipment, but leaves the details to the Department of Energy (DOE) to explain in a rule in late December. “The details of the DOE rule are what are going to cause some drama,” says George Gross, emeritus professor of electrical engineering at the University of Illinois in Urbana-Champaign and a former long-time Pacific Gas & Electric Company engineer and manager. “I was surprised that the community did not exactly scream, ‘We are all going to be overwhelmed.’” But that may be because they see enough latitude for purchasing what they need, Gross adds, even as the shape of the supply chain will change. Power Inverters and Grid Security Power inverters are a key component for converting DC electricity from sources such as solar farms or long-term battery storage into AC electricity for the grid. In 2025, industry group Green Power Denmark detected hidden communications channels in some circuit boards bound for installation on power inverters. In a different incident, Célistine Oosting, a security researcher at the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability disclosure publicly exposed credentials allowing firmware updates to her parents’ solar panels. And while there is no public proof of a Trojan horse-type attack on an electrical grid in the U.S. or EU, the vulnerabilities show how enterprising hackers could open a back door. The risks extend beyond inverters to other components in the long-distance transmission part of the electrical grid collectively called bulk-power equipment. For example, in 2015 and 2016, hackers used existing weaknesses in Ukrainian electrical equipment to cause blackouts, including by controlling switchboards and circuit breakers. The U.S. DOE has been wrestling with how to handle grid hacking since before then, and other countries have since developed their own approaches. India’s energy authority has required laboratory malware testing of foreign components since 2020, among other measures. Japan’s equivalent authority has since 2024 required a 30-day advance screening before approving the installation of certain power equipment. The European purchasing decision, which does not apply to nationally- or privately-funded projects, may still force energy companies to replace 4 to 5 gigawatts’ worth of planned bulk-power equipment purchasing from Chinese suppliers from now to 2030, energy consultancy Woods Mackenzie estimated in July. That’s about 14 to 18 percent of the EU’s planned purchases over that period. Inverter manufacturers, renewable energy suppliers, and investment bankers met with EU officials in June to discuss their ability to replace that Chinese manufacturing capacity. The upshot: It is possible, but will be slow and costly. EU and U.S. Power Supply Chains EU and U.S. power supply companies are trying to update their supply chains even though they know the rules will probably continue to change in the short term. Some are trying to make those rules better suit them. For example, inverter manufacturer Fronius, in Wels, Austria, warned in June that replacing the Chinese components in its supply chain could take a year. It also advocated for the EU to enact an outright ban on new Chinese bulk-power components rather than just saying it won’t pay for them. That way Fronius and other companies in its position can justify the upfront investment in new, costlier suppliers. In September, the DOE requested public comment on its rule-making. Some requested clarification of what components DOE would consider “associated with” bulk-power equipment, and recommended keeping the list as narrow as possible to address only elements that allow control of grid components. At least one supply chain verification firm proposed requiring risk-based sampling and physical tests, rather than relying on paper-based statements from importers. The firm also argued that the DOE could define a system in which accredited laboratories that already evaluate other sensitive equipment such as aerospace components compete to provide testing services, to add security while keeping down costs for utilities. Other companies are not waiting around for new rules to make new plans. SMA Solar, in Niestetal, Germany, estimates it stands to gain around 10 percent share of Europe’s utility-scale market, its chief executive said in August, thanks to the fact that it only depends on China for a small percentage of its supply chain (around 2 to 4 percent), and has the capacity to ramp up EU production. Some U.S. suppliers also stand to benefit. Unico, which is headquartered in Franksville, Wisconsin, designs and assembles a range of energy equipment, including inverters, in the U.S. The company, which also has a presence in the EU, designs its own printed circuit board assemblies, field-programmable gate array-based control loops, and magnetic components including inductors and transformers in-house. This allows Unico to retain direct control over firmware development and system architecture. The company does import components from abroad, but already made a point of carefully reviewing its supply chain. “We’re always looking at the sources of supply, traceability, qualification, and commercial scale capacity,” says Unico CEO Mike Canada. “And we’re always looking at the geopolitical risk, and we work to keep those high-risk areas out of our supply chain.” Canada says it’s hard to tell just how long it will take for U.S. and European companies to replace banned components from their purchasing and existing installations, given the complexity of the supply chain. But the work is evolving, as governments make their concerns more explicit. For example, “cybersecurity is becoming a key aspect in our purchasing decisions,” Canada says. The most direct way for some of Unico’s competitors to gain trust and access to the market may be to establish a new U.S. manufacturing presence, but that will take time. Right now grid operators are eager to build as fast as they can to keep up with exploding electricity demand from sectors including AI data centers. For the foreseeable future, Canada says, “There’s a substantial opportunity being an American engineering and manufacturing company.”

articles.title: Edge AI for Smart Cities: From Insight to Cognitive Action
articles.description: This white paper explains how edge AI and physical AI help cities move beyond passive monitoring. It shows how urban infrastructure can sense, reason, and act on real-time conditions across public safety, mobility, and infrastructure management. What you will learn about: How the shift from smart cities to cognitive cities depends on infrastructure that reasons and acts, rather than infrastructure that only monitors. Why edge AI supports low-latency decisions, keeps sensitive data within city boundaries, and reduces dependency on centralized cloud infrastructure. How computer vision, multimodal sensing, and generative and agentic systems work together to support public safety, mobility, and infrastructure applications. How a tiered edge architecture assigns monitoring, planning, and action tasks across the far edge, regional, and cloud layers, and what durability, security, and interoperability requirements this places on hardware and software. Download this free whitepaper now!

articles.title: A new way to detect stabilizing properties of optical devices
articles.description: In optical fibers, chips and other light-guiding devices, minor defects can scatter photons and disrupt their path. A new study demonstrates a way to reveal properties which, in certain systems, help light wave behavior withstand such flaws. The method could help speed up the search for new kinds of electronics and optical technologies, and contribute to more reliable quantum devices.
